analysis.one_liner: Required labels on foods made with or fed genetically engineered ingredients.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its introduction in May 2002 it sat in House committees until the two-year term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made companies label any food containing or produced with genetically engineered material, including animals raised on genetically engineered feed. It also set civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation and allowed ordinary citizens to sue violators. The House referred it to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who want to know whether their food contains genetically engineered ingredients. The bill would have put the words 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' on the front of packaged foods and required testing along the supply chain to verify labels were accurate [S2][S3]. It also benefited organic and non-GE producers, whose foods would stand out clearly to buyers, and it exempted certified organic foods from testing requirements [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food shoppers; organic and non-GE producers

how_it_helps.text: Foods containing or produced with genetically engineered material would be misbranded unless labeled with a conspicuous 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' notice sized like nutrition labels [S2][S3].
Regulations would require periodic testing of foods moving through the distribution chain to verify label accuracy, using the best available detection technology [S2][S3].
The bill set civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation and authorized citizen lawsuits against violators or against the agency if it failed to enforce the rules [S2][S3].

The bill's findings cited consumer concerns about allergen transfer, environmental risks, religious and ethical dietary restrictions, and the fact that major trading partners such as the EU, Japan, and China had adopted mandatory labeling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers and meat, poultry, and dairy producers, who would bear relabeling and periodic testing costs. Under the bill's broad definition, an animal fed genetically engineered corn or soy counts as 'produced with' genetic engineering, so a very large share of meat, dairy, eggs, and processed foods would have needed new labels [S3]. Any added compliance costs could be passed on in food prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food makers and GE crop/seed sellers

drawbacks.text: The definition is extremely broad: because animals fed genetically engineered feed count as 'produced with' it, foods with no detectable genetically engineered material — like meat, milk, and eggs — would still require labels, which critics called misleading and costly [S3].
Food companies and some scientists have long argued such labels imply a safety risk without evidence and add compliance costs across the supply chain (widely reported industry position).
The citizen-suit provision would let any person sue alleged violators, which could generate litigation even where the agency considered the issue minor [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers who care about knowing what is in their food, the bill delivered real information at essentially no taxpayer cost, since companies bear the labeling expense. The honest trade-off is scope: by counting animals fed GE feed, the bill would have labeled a huge share of the food supply, including products with no detectable engineered material, and the relabeling and testing costs would be real. Its own text recognized this tension by allowing a 1% tolerance for accidental contamination and exempting organic and restaurant foods [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The House sent the bill to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees and their subcommittees in May and June 2002, and neither ever held a hearing or vote, so it died when the term ended in January 2003 [S5].

narrative.text: Kucinich introduced the bill on May 22, 2002 with 24 original cosponsors; it was referred to the Agriculture Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S1][S3][S5].

In early June 2002 it was referred to subcommittees — Health, Livestock and Horticulture, and Farm Commodities and Risk Management — and the record shows no hearings, markups, or floor action afterward [S5].
The bill gathered 38 cosponsors, all Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on [S4].
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003, and the bill was never reported out of committee, so it did not carry over [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers and sellers of genetically engineered seed, who faced no labeling mandate, plus the committee chairs who never had to schedule a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food makers and GE seed sellers

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled House never acted on it.

industries.note: Under the bill, nearly any product with a genetically engineered ingredient — or an ingredient from an animal fed GE feed — would carry a mandatory front-of-package notice, forcing relabeling across a huge share of the food supply. The bill's testing rules also applied to them along the distribution chain [S3].

Mandatory labels would make genetic engineering visible to shoppers at the register for the first time, which the industry has long opposed on marketing grounds. The bill's broad 'produced with' definition reached their seed traits even in meat and dairy, where the material is not detectable [S3].

Because the bill counts animals fed GE feed as 'produced with' engineered material, most conventional meat, dairy, and eggs would need labels even though no engineered material is detectable in them. Producers relying on guaranties from feed suppliers were shielded from penalties, and accidental contamination was excused [S3].

Certified organic foods were exempt from the testing requirements, and a clear labeling regime would make their products stand out to consumers who want to avoid GE ingredients — a competitive advantage [S3].
Food served in restaurants was explicitly exempt from the labeling requirement, leaving that sector largely unaffected [S2][S3].
